item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I was thinking further about this essay, and I want to talk about jargon and vocabulary for a moment.

Sometimes we think that using bigger words conveys a more scientific tone, but that's not the case. As A Random Day points out, good clinical tone is succinct, using as few words as possible to describe situation at hand in language that is as unambiguous as possible. The reason a larger vocabulary is employed is because the extra words provides extra meaning.

Take directions and positions of objects on or in a mass, for example. How do you describe them? Left and right are fine, and well defined. In fact, using words like "dextral" and "sinistral" are not recommended, because they have other connotations of handedness that aren't warranted. Inside and outside? Forward and back? Top and bottom? Well, it depends. If you're describing something that is close or far away from a reference point, "proximal" and "distal" are defined as that exactly. If it's something with an outer and inner layer, then "cortical" and "medullary" describe them exactly, while "inside" and "outside" are not as clear. Similarly, when describing organisms, you've got directions like cranial/caudal and anterior/posterior which are well defined directions on your typical bilateral animal.

But, for example, I recently ran across the phrase "the distal end of the gastrointestinal tract" recently. This is bad clinical tone. First, distal to what? We aren't given the proper reference point. Caudal and posterior are much more precise terms for that end. However, we actually have a much more clinical term for this, one that is succinct and removes all ambiguity about what we are referring to: the anus. It's also far shorter.

We should remember: jargon and vocabulary should be used to assist us in being as clear and concise as possible. It is not about using ten words where five will do; it's about knowing which one word describes what might colloquially take five.

item.content:encoded: Alright, taking thedeadlymoose and Kapitano's critiques into account, I have altered the first tenet of the Qualitative Description segment. Instead of 'one trait, one adjective', it is now 'what you see is what you describe'. This tenet is focused on ensuring that the description avoids phrases like "piercing blue eyes" or "has been noted to be very protective of what he considers the innocent".

item.content:encoded: I think we're using different definitions of evocative. I agree that your examples are all good clinical tone. However, something like "SCP-ZZZZ bears the rugged good looks of New Zealand actor Russell Crowe" is bad tone, and the sort of evocative nature I suggest we avoid.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This is right, or at least better:

In case of containment breach, contact Dr Smith

In this case nothing is probably best here. It doesn't make a lot of sense to mention specific people in the containment procedures, job titles are almost always better, because individual people can be incapacitated, unavailable, or replaced but job titles combined with clear chains of command and succession will be evergreen. If you rewrite this as:

In case of containment breach notify the project lead.

This seems like such a no-brainer that it would have to be standard procedure for all containment, and therefore doesn't belong in special containment procedures.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The documentation should not be evocative, even as it describes an evocative situation.

I'm going to have to disagree with you vigorously. Clinical tone can, and should, be evocative, since the goal is to accurately and concisely describe an object, situation, or event. If, by the time they're done reading, your audience can't visualize — or at least conceptualize — what you're describing, you've failed at doing clinical tone.

Sentences like "SCP-XXXX is a rubber sphere, approximately the same size as a baseball." and "SCP-YYYY resembles a steam locomotive." and "SCP-ZZZZ has the appearance of New Zealander actor Russell Crowe." are all perfectly good clinical tone. Describing these things with quantitative measurements would both require more words and be less evocative, and so should only be done if there's an absolute need to do so.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Guides to creative writing are full of vague abstractions, and pieces of advice which are generally applicable - except when they're not. I think, rather than trying to come with principles and writing to them, we should give examples of bad SCP writing, suggest a re-write, and say why the re-write works better for the genre.

This may not tell us what good writing looks like, but it should help identify features of bad SCP writing to avoid.

These are wrong:

If SCP-XXXX breaches containment, it is absolutely imperative to contact Dr Smith immediately.
If a breach occurs, please try to find Dr Smith to ask him what to do.
Should SCP-XXXX escape, Dr Smith will provide instructions for recapture.

This is right, or at least better:

In case of containment breach, contact Dr Smith.

Why? Because imperatives should be neither softened by politeness, nor modified with modulations of urgency, nor converted to declaratives. When you give an order, just give the order. Brevity is nice, but that's a consequence of directness, not a goal in itself.

This is wrong, in many ways:

SCP-XXXX is a faroff, almost unreachable big mountain, always blanketed in heavy, black rain - even from cloudless skies.

This is IMHO better:

SCP-XXXX is a mountain located in ██████████, ███████. It is continuously subject to dense precipitation of an opaque, dark liquid. Though the liquid itself shows no anomalous properties, its source is unknown, and production uniform, regardless of cloud cover. Due to its size and remote location, SCP-XXXX cannot be contained. Current policy is to limit public awareness - see Document XXXX-A for details.

Why? "Faroff" is informal, "distant" formal. All mountains are big, so there's no need to specify it. Also "large" is for some reason seen as more "educated" than "big". "Blanketed" vs "Dense" - better to be literal than metaphorical. Having said that, we might say "cloud cover" is a dead metaphor, so acceptable.

"Precipitation" vs "rain" - it's not just that "precipitation" is the longer, sciencier word, it's that "rain" has associations (as opposed to connotations), whereas "precipitation" doesn't. A goth song might start "Today I awoke to the rain of blood", but "Today I awoke to the precipitation of blood"? Um, no.

"Cloudless skies" - it's a common collocation, but the issue isn't the skies - or that there's only one sky - but the clouds or their lack. Also, general advice, if you can imagine a phrase being used in bad poetry, it's probably best not to use it.

As for when to use a connecting dash…" - even from cloudless skies" is an afterthought, whereas " - see Document XXXX-A" is a way of connecting two sentences more closely than with a period.

You might disagree with all these examples. It's not an exact science.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I think something more along the lines of "remain objective and factual" is better. You want to remove language that indicates emotion, opinion, or speculation.

Words like shocking, surprising, filthy, carnage, beautiful, sexy, heartless should be avoided because they're all judgment calls. Describe what you have in front of you so that anyone, whether or not they share your values and priors, understands what they're dealing with.

Words like possibly, surmise, perhaps, probably should be considered potential red flags. They suggest that what is to follow is speculation, not rooted in physical evidence. Here, the show, don't tell mantra helps greatly, since when you show it, you provide evidence for it, and the situation becomes less subjective and more objective.

The documentation should not be evocative, even as it describes an evocative situation.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
A propos of nothing, clinical tone is something that (if I may be so bold) I do pretty well.

From SCP-1012: "Through Foundation efforts, Balaenoptera svalbardi became extinct in 1982, thereby decreasing the likelihood that the tone would inadvertently be generated in a location near the generation of other constituent tones." This is a clinical way of saying "the Foundation intentionally wiped out an entire species."

From SCP-089: "Following SCP-089-B’s placement of SCP-089-A in the cavity and the ignition of the inflammable materials, SCP-089-A will burn and be destroyed over a period of two to five hours." This sentence is intentionally separated from the reveal that SCP-089-A is a baby, and SCP-089-B is the baby's mother.

From SCP-1036: "sentient incorporeal entity". This is my terminology for a spirit that inhabits an idol.

From SCP-1844: "The pit, or an extradimensional space accessible through the pit, contains an indeterminate number of hostile entities, the escape of which is arrested by means of the containment regimen." (It's a gateway to hell.)

From SCP-1746: "Immediately after dropping the frozen dairy confection, Actor F3 is to adopt body language consistent with distress over loss of the dessert." (Part of the containment regimen requires a child to drop ice cream and cry about it. It sort of makes sense in context.)

From SCP-908: "The islet is a geographic anomaly; it is located in several different places at once." (Here, rather than use technical language, I decided that the appropriate tone was to be as matter-of-fact as possible about the subject.)

From SCP-2336: "a Type I or Type II tartarean entity". (Demons)

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
In the case of "die," I think it's more a question of specificity. Preventing animal cell death means a very different thing from preventing dying. "It prevents death" is just as nebulous as "it grants immortality." But otherwise, yes, words like "dying" and "death" are acceptable.

More generally, "the object is dead to you" is key to making the clinical tone work. If you can describe it in as matter-of-fact a way as possible while simply allowing the implications of the situation to do the heavy lifting of carrying the emotion of the piece, then you've got a story, SCP-style.

And let's not forget that SCP is a style. From the clinical tone, to the bureaucratic euphemisms, to the [DATA EXPUNGED], these are all tools to tell the story of an outfit who is both professional in its task of dealing with the paranormal, and at times jaded, overwhelmed, barely sufficient.

A good vocabulary helps immeasurably, as well. Knowing the different nuance in meaning between "die," "expire," "cease function," "terminate," or "no longer" is key, many times, to making a piece work.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
> 'die' is considered a non-clinical verb
It's perfectly clinical.

There's room for disagreement about how clinical or formal a word is. But I think we could use a collaborative list of colloquial words and phrases to avoid, and suggested scientific alternatives.

"Spectacles" is more formal than "glasses", but does that make "glasses" informal? Likewise "adolescent" and "teenager". Some skips use "regular" in the sense of "normal" or "default", but at least in the UK, this is very informal.

A related issue is the use of euphemisms masquerading as precise technical terms. E.g "Self-terminate" for "suicide", or "negative result" for "failure". In-universe, the Foundation would have its own brand of bureaucratic bullshit, but I'm not sure how much the authors should allow them to use it.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This is a pretty good essay, hitting lots of points that people typically ignore.

There are a few errors stopping me from upvoting:

One trait, one adjective:

This is not a basic rule of qualitative clinical tone, nor, indeed, a rule relating to clinical tone at all.

I think what you're trying to get at is an extension of "the object is dead to you", so no descriptions that seem flowery or flattering or impressive or otherwise trying to evoke an emotion. "Piercing" and "deep" aren't bad because they're an additional word, they're bad because they're trying to make the reader swoon.

"Simplicity is paramount" is also misleading. Simplicity is a good goal, but it isn't the issue you're addressing — and most examples you give are very much not simple, but are wordy and complex for effect.

Also:

One of those quirks is that 'die' is considered a non-clinical verb,

It's perfectly clinical. I think what you're getting at here is that it's an example of a common strategy to get across an aesthetic impression of clinical tone. Optionally, people may replace words like "die" to get across further detachment. But if someone thinks 'die' works better for their piece, it very well might — and it's not considered non-clinical.

I know these are nitpicky issues, but if this essay's gonna get linked to people regularly, I gotta hold it to a high standard!

(Might have more later. Am a bit sick.)

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Well-written (and not just the parts that compliment me). With respect to the discussion of 1512 and Vickers hardness, perhaps it's worth pointing out that Vickers hardness is an actual scientific measurement standard, used properly here. (In contrast, compare SCP-1844 which uses a measurement in centiakivas, which is a fictional SI unit of measurement but which is intended to make sense in context.)

Another aspect of clinical tone that is perhaps worth discussing is the use of passive voice. ("…the lotion is to be placed in the basket…" rather than "… put the lotion in the basket…" Generally speaking, passive voice is something that style guides frown upon. But in the SCP context, it works because it helps de-personalize the narrative.

Edit:
Don't know why I didn't think to mention this before, but I'll add it now: if you want to learn to write using clinical tone, read samples of documents that are in clinical tone. Read autopsy reports. Read plane crash reports. Read military after-action reports. One of the most chilling documents I've ever read that was written in clinical tone is the Hurricane Katrina warning bulletin from the National Weather Service.

item.content:encoded:
"high-pitched whimpering gasps" is one trait with one adjective and one adverb.

Is it? "Whimpering" is an active participle, and thus an adjective. "Pitched" is a passive participle, and thus another adjective, in this case modified by a third adjective.

Your principle that one trait is allowed only one adjective is a reasonable guideline, but this example shows it's not an absolute rule.

I've mentioned this in chat a few times, but I just want to thank A Random Day for choosing SCP-847 to be a part of this guide. Maintaining clinical tone was incredibly important throughout the piece. Heck, I imagined the Foundation researcher charged with writing this as thinking, "Oh god, stick to the facts, stick to the facts, don't think about her," throughout the entire piece. Keeping the object dead to you in the prose was key, because the visceral effect was anything but.

The amount of time I spent asking myself if "high-pitched whimpering gasps and adopting more provocative poses" was a reasonable way to describe it trying to come on to a man was huge. Thank you for noticing that.

item.content:encoded:
Like anything else, you're never going to please everybody- The key is that your audience as a whole is able to understand the idea well enough for it to work. 2323 does that, hence all the upvotes.

Its a thing in visual art, too- Dada aside, the goal is always to have an image be comprehensible at a glance (even abstract works aim to convey a general emotion or impact upon initial viewing). It's one thing to have to explain why there's a giant bird building a nest on a building- its another if you have to explain to everyone that the picture is a giant bird building a nest on a building.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
But if the reader has to ask clarifying questions about what's actually written on the page, that's the author's fault.

I am going to disagree with this a bit. Sometimes some readers just aren't going to get it, and you risk over explaining to the majority if you try to explain everything to everybody.

For example, I have gone over SCP-2323's comments multiple times and I still don't see how I can address some of the questions there, which seem to be caused by a couple of readers not understanding what memes are really supposed to be or not understanding that the Foundation primarily contains things that are anomalous. I can't actually explain memetics or the Foundation in the article as these topics are well outside the scope of an SCP article. The article itself is highly successful and it would probably be stupid to try to "fix" it when it clearly ain't broke anyway.

Sometimes people are going to ask clarifying questions that aren't the author's fault because they missed something when they read it, because they aren't familiar with something that is key but outside the scope of the article, or because they simply failed to make a connection.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Excellent essay, spot-on advice here.

+ One additional observation/suggestion for the 'Clinical ≠ Verbose' section
- One additional observation/suggestion for the 'Clinical ≠ Verbose' section:

Word choice is also about eliminating ambiguity while saying things indirectly. As Mark Twain put it, "The difference between the right word and almost the right word is the difference between 'lightning' and 'lightning bug'."

For instance, saying that the gas "makes people immortal" doesn't describe the full range of effects, and actually provides some false information, because that's not really what this does.

The phrase "animal cells" instead of "people" or "organisms" tells us that the effect isn't limited to humans, and doesn't affect an organism as a whole- only the cells. The individual pieces of an organism are simply "unable to cease life function", no matter their current state. Effects pointedly not listed: "enhanced regeneration", "ability to function effectively despite massive trauma", "pain resistance", and "immunity to infection".

By picking just the right words to say what he wanted, Kalinin describes a multilayered and disturbing effect, without directly describing the vast majority of its effects at all.
